solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

definitions.note: plural noun for a mass noun; blossom is a tree's flowers taken together

indicators.note: something returned goes back the way it came, so the letters run backwards
to accept something is to take it in, so one piece receives another inside it

blocks.note: a mob is a disorderly crowd
a defeat is a loss

explanation.surface: A beaten crowd heads home carrying flowers, perhaps after a lost match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Accepting defeat' reads like a gracious loser, but 'accepting' is the container signal: the turned-round mob takes the loss inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Blossom names the flowers on a fruit tree or shrub collectively, so it stands for flowers in bloom.

clue.text: Teaching graduate with job gets support for retirement

blocks.note: a BEd is a Bachelor of Education degree
a post is a job or position

explanation.surface: A newly qualified teacher lands a job and starts paying into a pension.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Support for retirement' sounds like a pension, but retiring here means going to bed; BEd is the Bachelor of Education degree held by many teachers.
explanation.definitionFit: Retiring for the night means going to bed, and the posts at its corners hold up the frame where you sleep.

blocks.note: O is the standard abbreviation for old
U is the standard abbreviation for university
St is the abbreviation for street, so streets are Sts

explanation.surface: Students are thrown out of an ancient university and onto its streets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'From' is only a link here, joining the definition to the wordplay rather than telling you to remove anything.
explanation.definitionFit: To oust someone is to force them out of a place or position, the same action as expelling them.

clue.text: Explanations lost on us unfortunately, first person overwhelmed

indicators.note: things that go unfortunately go wrong, so the letters fall into a different order
to be overwhelmed is to be engulfed, so one piece is swallowed up inside the other

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged
I is the first person singular pronoun

explanation.surface: Someone complains that the explanations went over everyone's heads, and the speaker was left swamped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Overwhelmed' reads as the speaker being swamped, but it tells you the pronoun is buried inside the rearranged phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Solutions are answers that resolve a problem or puzzle, which is what explanations provide.

clue.text: Leaders of most unions stand in corridors singing, perhaps

indicators.note: leaders go at the front, so only the opening letter of each word is kept

blocks.note: the initial letters of these five words

explanation.surface: Union bosses stand in hallways, maybe chanting or singing on a picket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' marks the definition as an example: singing is one kind of what the answer names.
explanation.definitionFit: Singing is one example of music, alongside instrumental playing, so the definition gives a member of the class.

blocks.note: an imp is a mischievous child or sprite
an IOU ('I owe you') is a written promise to pay a debt

explanation.surface: A disrespectful rascal hands over a pile of written promises instead of cash.
explanation.walkthrough: IOU is the familiar note saying 'I owe you', so several of them are promises to pay.
explanation.definitionFit: Impious means lacking respect for religion or sacred things, which is close to irreverent.

indicators.note: surrounding something means enclosing it on all sides, so one piece goes around the other

blocks.note: India is the Indian subcontinent's main country, often just called the subcontinent
one's written without its apostrophe

explanation.surface: A large region of Asia wraps around one's homeland.
explanation.walkthrough: Crosswords ignore apostrophes, so 'one's' supplies the letters ONES, which sit inside the subcontinent's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Indonesia is a nation of islands in South East Asia, so it is an example of a country.

definitions.note: adjective for numbers, as in a prime number

blocks.note: first meaning: prepare something, as you would a pump or a wall before painting
second meaning: divisible only by itself and one, like these two numbers

explanation.surface: It reads like preparing for a date or a bus number.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For' is just the link; '11 or 13, say' gives examples of a kind of number, hence the 'say'.
explanation.definitionFit: To prime is to prepare in advance, and a prime number has no divisors other than itself and one.

clue.text: Watching former pupil starting a tennis match

blocks.note: OB stands for old boy, a former pupil of a school
every tennis point begins with a serve

explanation.surface: Someone watches an old school pupil open a game of tennis.
explanation.walkthrough: An old boy (OB) is a British term for a former pupil of a school.
explanation.definitionFit: Observing means looking at closely or noticing, the same as watching.

indicators.note: being in something means sitting inside it, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: a shed is a small outbuilding
an ear is a single head of corn, so just some of it

explanation.surface: Someone cuts down a portion of corn stored in a barn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some corn' is not a hidden-word signal: it gives an ear, one head of corn.
explanation.definitionFit: Sheared is the past tense of shear, to clip or cut, as with sheep's wool or metal.

indicators.note: something off is not right or has gone bad, so the letters are out of order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A spy gave away the codes and slipped quietly away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slid off' reads as a getaway, but 'off' is the signal to rearrange the two words before it.
explanation.definitionFit: To disclose is to make known something previously secret, which is what revealing means.

indicators.note: tearing the cover off strips away the outside front, so the opening letter goes

blocks.note: tissue is a thin soft paper

explanation.surface: Someone rips the cover off a paper magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: The cover is the first letter only; 'paper' wants to be the newspaper, but it is tissue paper.
explanation.definitionFit: An issue is a single edition of a periodical, so one copy of a magazine is an issue.

definitions.note: prepositional phrase, read as two words ON SET

blocks.note: first meaning: an assault, the start of hostilities
second meaning: split into two words, being where filming happens

explanation.surface: It suggests a violent incident during a television broadcast.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark warns that the second half is playful: actors in a studio are 'on set', and the two words run together.
explanation.definitionFit: An onset is an attack or assault, an old military sense, as well as the beginning of something.

indicators.note: something dubious is questionable or not straight, so the letters are not to be trusted in this order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A football fan blames the referee for awarding a dodgy corner kick.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is about football, with 'giver' looking like the referee; it is the definition, and the corner and ref are the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: To confer is to grant or bestow an honour or gift, so whoever does that is a giver.

clue.text: Slow movers jog back alongside French river, starting to sweat

indicators.note: going back means travelling the opposite way, so these letters are read in reverse
the start of a word is its opening letter, so only that one is kept

blocks.note: to trot is to jog
the Oise is a river in northern France
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: Sluggish runners jog beside a river in France and begin to perspire.
explanation.walkthrough: The Oise is a tributary of the Seine, a river crosswords use often after the Seine itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Tortoises are reptiles famous for moving slowly, as in the fable of the tortoise and the hare.

indicators.note: putting things around moves them about, so the letters are mixed up

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A flagpole needs a ring fitted round it to hold the flag.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put around' looks like a container signal wrapping the ring round something, but nothing is enclosed: it tells you to move the letters around.
explanation.definitionFit: The Red Ensign is the flag flown by British merchant ships, a red field with the Union Jack in the corner.

clue.text: Dismiss fool over hot itchy fabric

indicators.note: in a down clue, over means placed above, so the first piece sits on top of what follows

blocks.note: to sack someone is to dismiss them from a job
a clot is a British word for a fool
H is the abbreviation for hot, as on taps

explanation.surface: An employer fires an idiot over a hot, scratchy garment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clot' is British slang for a stupid person; 'over' only places the first piece above the next in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Sackcloth is coarse rough cloth worn as penance, famously uncomfortable against the skin.

clue.text: Current elected house rejected epic poem

indicators.note: something rejected is sent back, so these letters go in the opposite direction

blocks.note: I is the symbol for electric current
the Dáil is the elected lower house of the Irish parliament

explanation.surface: The sitting parliament turns down a lengthy poem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Elected house' looks like a general phrase for parliament; it is the Dáil, the elected chamber of Ireland's parliament.
explanation.definitionFit: Homer's Iliad is the ancient Greek narrative about the Trojan War, the archetype of the genre.

clue.text: Without preparation, I’m on time, you heard

indicators.note: what you hear is spoken, so the phrase is judged by its sound rather than spelling

blocks.note: on time is prompt, followed by you

explanation.surface: Someone boasts of being punctual despite not having prepared anything.
explanation.walkthrough: 'You heard' reads as 'you heard me', but it is the sound signal; 'I'm prompt, you' said quickly runs into one word.
explanation.definitionFit: An impromptu speech or performance is done on the spur of the moment, with no rehearsal.

indicators.note: the essence of a thing is its core, so only the central letters are kept

blocks.note: to rid is to free, as in rid of
the two letters at the heart of the word

explanation.surface: Trips made on complimentary fuel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Free' looks like an anagram signal or a price; it gives RID, as in being freed of something.
explanation.definitionFit: Rides are trips taken in or on a vehicle or animal, so they are journeys.

clue.text: Regret insult on the radio? Nonsense

indicators.note: radio carries only sound, so the words are taken as they are spoken

blocks.note: to rue is to regret and a barb is a cutting remark

explanation.surface: A broadcaster regrets an insult made on air, and someone calls it nonsense.
explanation.walkthrough: Rhubarb is British slang for nonsense, from the word actors murmur to sound like background chatter.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang rhubarb means rubbish or meaningless talk, an idiomatic sense of the vegetable.

clue.text: Fake glass delivered for celebratory drink

indicators.note: a speech is delivered aloud, so what matters is how the words sound when spoken

blocks.note: a sham is a fake and a pane is a sheet of glass

explanation.surface: Imitation glassware is brought round for a toast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Delivered' wants to mean brought to the door; it means spoken, as a speech is delivered.
explanation.definitionFit: Champagne is the sparkling wine traditionally opened to mark celebrations and toast successes.

clue.text: A genre novel with lead character in Sussex infuriates

indicators.note: the lead character of a word is its first letter, so only that one is kept
novel means new, so the letters are made into a fresh arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written
the opening letter of the county

explanation.surface: A type of fiction whose protagonist lives in Sussex makes readers furious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' and 'lead character' both pretend to be about books; the first rearranges, the second takes one letter from the English county of Sussex.
explanation.definitionFit: To enrage someone is to make them extremely angry, which is what infuriating them does.

indicators.note: something criminal is crooked and wrong, so the letters are bent out of order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A crook carried on his business without the authorities spotting it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Criminal' looks like the subject of the sentence; it is the signal to rearrange the next word.
explanation.definitionFit: Flying under the radar means escaping detection, an idiom for going unobserved by anyone watching.

clue.text: Time husband at last wrote thank you letter

indicators.note: at last means at the very end, so only the final letter is kept

blocks.note: T is the abbreviation for time
H is the abbreviation for husband
the final letter of the word
ta is informal British for thank you

explanation.surface: After a while a husband finally sends a thank-you note.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At last wrote' reads as finally writing; it takes the last letter of 'wrote', and 'ta' is a casual British thanks.
explanation.definitionFit: Theta is the eighth character of the Greek alphabet, so it is one alphabet symbol.

clue.text: Removes police officer restraining a third of offenders

indicators.note: a third of a nine-letter word is three letters, taken from its front
to restrain is to hold in, so one piece is held inside the other

blocks.note: DS is a detective sergeant
the first letters of the word, three of its nine, a third of it

explanation.surface: An officer takes people away while holding back some of the criminals.
explanation.walkthrough: DS (detective sergeant) is the usual crossword police officer, alongside DI and PC.
explanation.definitionFit: To doff is to take off an item of clothing, especially a hat, so it means removes.

clue.text: Section of proof Fermat’s put forward

indicators.note: a section is a part cut out of something larger, so the letters lie within the next words

blocks.note: runs across the two words

explanation.surface: Part of Fermat's famous proof is presented for consideration.
explanation.walkthrough: Fermat's Last Theorem was famous for a proof he claimed but never wrote down; the answer spans the join between the two words.
explanation.definitionFit: To offer an idea or proposal is to present it for others to consider, which is putting it forward.

definitions.note: an example: a martin is a bird, hence something that flies

blocks.note: first meaning: a martin is a small swallow-like bird, so one thing that takes to the air
second meaning: a printed handbill handed out to advertise something

explanation.walkthrough: Martin looks like a man's name owning a leaflet; it is the bird, and the possessive stands for 'is'. The question mark flags the example.
explanation.definitionFit: A bird that flies is a flier, and a printed advertising handout is also called a flier or flyer.

indicators.note: some means a part rather than all, so the letters are a portion of the next word

blocks.note: sits in the middle of the word

explanation.surface: A few copycats get to their feet, perhaps to confess.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer sits inside one word, starting at its fifth letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To arise is to get up from sitting or lying, an older or formal way of saying stand.

blocks.note: a machine that is off is not working
a spring is a natural source of water, like a well

explanation.surface: Kids are off sick from school, not feeling well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Well' wants to mean healthy; it is the noun, a source of water.
explanation.definitionFit: Offspring are a person's or animal's descendants, especially their sons and daughters.

clue.text: Lower down Scottish mountain dine on starter of haggis

indicators.note: the starter comes first in a meal, so the first letter alone is kept

blocks.note: ben is the Scottish word for mountain, as in Ben Nevis
to dine is to eat
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: Down from a Scottish peak, someone eats haggis as a first course.
explanation.walkthrough: Haggis is Scotland's national dish of sheep's offal; 'on' simply places the next pieces after the mountain in this across entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Beneath means in a lower position or underneath, the same as lower down.

blocks.note: first meaning: old-fashioned conventional types, in dated slang
second meaning: numbers raised to the power of two, one specific power

explanation.walkthrough: The possessive stands for 'are'; 'powers' reads as political might but is mathematical.
explanation.definitionFit: Squares is slang for conventional unhip people, and in arithmetic a square is a number raised to the second power.
